claims.text: Ultra-high-vacuum processing with active impurity control will minimize oxygen and nitrogen uptake in a refractory high-entropy alloy.
Reducing oxygen and nitrogen uptake will suppress interstitial-induced phase segregation during thermal exposure.
Suppressing interstitial-induced phase segregation will improve elevated-temperature mechanical strength relative to conventional processing.
A conventionally arc-melted Ti–Zr–Hf–V–Ta refractory HEA has a BCC structure.
Conventionally produced refractory HEAs typically contain trace oxygen and nitrogen impurities.
Trace oxygen and nitrogen impurities promote nanoscale phase segregation upon aging in the proposed refractory HEA.
Ultra-high-vacuum melting or sintering with in situ gettering can reduce oxygen and nitrogen incorporation during synthesis.
Impurity control will reduce impurity-induced nanoscale segregated phases or interstitial-rich regions at grain boundaries.
Reducing grain-boundary segregation will produce a more stable solid-solution microstructure.
Interstitial oxygen and nitrogen drive local phase segregation and softening during thermal aging.
Lower interstitial concentrations will preserve solid-solution strengthening and microstructural stability at elevated temperature.
After aging at 700°C, the impurity-controlled alloy will have higher yield strength than an otherwise identical conventionally processed alloy.
After aging at 700°C, the impurity-controlled alloy will exhibit less softening than the conventionally processed baseline.
A conventionally arc-melted baseline without enhanced impurity control shows significant age softening caused by interstitial-induced phase segregation.
The expected improvement is bounded to refractory HEAs operated near 700°C over service-relevant exposure durations.

Failure to achieve a statistically significant improvement of more than approximately 10–20% in yield-strength retention or reduced microstructural degradation after aging at 700°C would falsify the hypothesis.
